limitations: Nothing here has been printed, handled or played. The fits, wall thicknesses and overhang margins are measurements taken on the exact CAD solids and predictions for a 0.4 mm nozzle at 0.2 mm layers.

The verification pipeline ran for 1126.08 s and FINISHED EVERY CHECK. Result: PASS, exit 0. All 51 geometry checks passed; none was left unverified and none failed. Measured in this run: all 24 printed parts cleared the mesh gate, the 45-degree overhang gate and the 0.80 mm wall-thickness gate at a 0.4 mm nozzle; the 204-occurrence assembly validates and reports no interference; and check_fit, check_layout and both spec checks returned clean. Both corrected Venus parts are among those that passed every gate -- part_world_venus_sol measured 0 of 160,826 wall samples below 0.80 mm and 0 unsupported overhang regions. Three checks were not run and are recorded as not run rather than passed: check_mount and check_power, because no bought part and no powered system is declared, and check_motion, which the operator's motion policy switched off for this build, so motion is unverified. This matters because the previous run in this correction chain did NOT finish: its wall-thickness check on part_world_venus_sol was cut off as the 83rd and last step when the shared 600-second geometry allowance ran out, and it was handed over as an unverified prototype. That exact check is the one completed above. As the last correction in the chain, this run states it in one place: verification is now complete for every part of the set. Even so, this build is not claimed to be print-ready -- nothing here has been printed, and print readiness is a claim about the physical world that no CAD gate can make.
Motion verification is switched off for this build and is recorded as unverified rather than passed. Nothing in the set moves relative to anything else in any case.

Venus is drawn from radar, not from light. Its surface is under an opaque atmosphere, so the only picture of it is the Magellan global radar mosaic, and the rings this piece is built from are stylised silhouettes of the major highland and lowland provinces at the accuracy a 16.53 mm globe can hold -- not Magellan mapping. What they claim is that Venus has one long equatorial highland, a handful of smaller ones and three broad lowland plains; they do not claim any boundary is where the spacecraft put it. Aphrodite Terra's sweep is the one shape on the globe a reader can check against the image.

None of the reference's texture survives, and none of it is faked. The mosaic is dominated by fine filamentary radar brightness -- tesserae, lava channels, fracture belts, the ragged look of beaten gold -- and one degree of arc is 0.1443 mm on this globe while the 0.4 mm nozzle needs 2.77 degrees, so a filament a few tens of kilometres wide is about a fifth of one nozzle width. The piece carries the continents and the plains and none of the texture: it is a simplified map of the reference, not the reference. No stippling and no fine ribs stand in for it, because the set's material rules forbid deliberate grit and at this size it would print as noise.

One whole Venusian province is drawn and cannot be seen. Venus's axis is tipped 177.36 degrees, which puts the planet's north pole into the collar the globe stands in, so Ishtar Terra -- which runs from Venusian +54 to +76 -- lands entirely inside that collar on both armies, and 36 per cent of Atalanta Planitia goes the same way. Ishtar is not absent from the plastic: 3.04 mm3 of beige survives above the disc's own cut and prints inside the collar where nothing can see it, so whoever loads the printer will find a beige body with no picture on it. Neither province was dropped and neither is a fault: the reason they are invisible is the inversion the set carries on purpose. cad/measure/venus-atlas-resolution.md measures it province by province.

Venus's beige highlands separate only 20.2 of 255 greyscale levels from its sunflower-yellow globe in the canonical renders -- the thinnest marking separation anywhere in this set, and below the 21.8 this set rejected on Mercury as invisible. It reads here for two measured reasons rather than one hoped-for one: Aphrodite Terra is a single continuous marking 117 degrees of longitude wide, 16.9 mm of arc and the longest in the set, and beige is a pink-cream against an amber so the boundary carries a hue step that greyscale does not count. A smaller feature in that pair of filaments would not read. White separates 27.9 and was measured and not taken, because white is already the brightest feature on Earth, Mars and Mercury. cad/measure/venus-tone-separation.md is the measurement.

Venus's globe and Saturn's are now neighbours in hue -- sunflower yellow #FFB549 against yellow #FFD834, 23.5 greyscale levels apart sealed and 11.2 as the renders show them. They are told apart by everything except colour: 9.47 mm of globe diameter, a 30 mm ring on one and nothing of the kind on the other, and the numerals 3 and 7. Rendered side by side at the product's own frame the silhouette carries it easily and the colour alone would not. cad/measure/venus-saturn-separation.md is that check.

Venus's globe also now shares sunflower yellow with the Sol star. That is stated rather than accidental: the amber was preferred to a new spool precisely because the set already carried it, and the two are never confused -- the star is a 36 mm square plinth lying flat on the board with two 18 mm flames rising off it.

Venus's four small highlands -- Alpha, Themis, Beta and Phoebe Regio -- are six-vertex rings 15 to 20 degrees across and read as small polygons at this size rather than as landforms. All four clear the nozzle, at 0.66 to 1.12 mm at their narrowest against a 0.40 mm floor, so none was dropped, none was shrunk to a dot and none was replaced by a circle.

Venus is one of the worlds that takes three filaments -- sunflower yellow, beige and cocoa brown -- where it used to take two. No new spool is needed: all three were already loaded for this set. Earth takes four; Mercury, Mars, Venus, Neptune, Saturn and Jupiter take three; Uranus alone takes two.

Aphrodite Terra spans more than 150 degrees of longitude, which is past the 72-degree limit of the outline tool that sweeps a ring into the globe, so the build draws it as two rings overlapping across 28 degrees whose union is the drawn ring exactly. No vertex moved and no width changed, and the built solids confirm the two come out as one continuous highland rather than two.

Mercury is the other world in the set that takes three filaments -- grey, cocoa brown and white. On this 13.78 mm globe the dark grey the plains used to carry is 21.8 of 255 greyscale levels away from the grey globe it sits on, and at that separation the patches are simply not visible. Cocoa brown measures 45.5 on the same test and the basin's white floor 36.9 against the globe and 114.3 against the rim. Black separates furthest at 139.6 and was deliberately not used: a black patch on a small grey ball reads as a hole in the print rather than as terrain.

Cocoa brown is a warm brown rather than a neutral grey, so at a glance Mercury's plains and Venus's lowlands sit in the same family of colour as Mars's dark continents and Saturn's and Jupiter's bands. That is the price of the separations above and it was paid deliberately.

Mercury's plains are drawn from a formula rather than from a map. Its albedo boundaries are genuinely soft and its plains are genuinely unnamed, so there is no silhouette anyone could check the model against. The Caloris basin's size and latitude are real; its longitude is a camera decision and is stated as one.

No crater field was added to Mercury, Mars or Venus. On each of the three the largest crater outside a named basin is one or two nozzle widths across, with no room for a rim and a floor inside it, so it would print as a pit one extrusion wide and read as a print defect. Caloris is the exception precisely because at 36 degrees of arc it is eleven nozzle widths across.

Mars's dark markings are the classical albedo map at the accuracy an eyepiece sketch has, not spacecraft mapping. Four vertices were moved to clear the nozzle; none of them moves an outline the eye reads. Mars's albedo is cocoa brown on a red globe, and those two filaments are only 1.88:1 apart in contrast -- under the 3:1 at which a difference in value reads as darkness rather than as a change of colour.

Mars's globe is sunk 2.00 mm into its disc and cut level with it, which at Mars's axial tilt removes about a seventh of the sphere and almost all of the south polar cap. The northern cap is the larger and more irregular of the two and that is measurable in the geometry, but it is not visible on the finished piece and is not claimed to be.

Earth's coastlines are a stylised silhouette atlas, not a survey coastline. Central America is one broad land bridge, and Japan, New Zealand, the Indonesian and Philippine arcs, the British Isles as a shape of their own, the Mediterranean's islands and Antarctica are not drawn; most are narrower than a 0.4 mm nozzle on a 16.70 mm globe, and each is listed with its reason in cad/measure/earth-atlas-resolution.md. One vertex was moved: the Australian outback's north-west corner came 0.33 mm inland. Nothing was dropped silently.

Earth's beige dryland is #F7E6DE, a very pale warm white. At this globe size it sits close in value to the white ice and an unprimed reader of the renders calls it light grey rather than sand. Both filaments were required to stay, so this is stated rather than fixed.
Earth and Neptune share the same blue filament. They are 5.19 mm apart in globe diameter, Earth carries green land and Neptune does not, and they carry different rank numerals.
The low side of Saturn's ring is thickened where its underside is carried down to the disc. That is what lets a tilted ring print without support, and it is visible from a seated eye.

The star's two flames are slimmer than the design that was handed in. The feet were narrowed to 6.00 mm and brought inboard so each flame stands on solid flange and prints without support; their 18 mm height, their outward lean and their taper are unchanged.

The review renders under cad/snap/ are drawn by a tool that encodes colour twice, so in those images every mid-tone is lifted: Mars's and Venus's cocoa brown appears as a light ochre and Venus's amber globe appears paler than the filament is. The colours sealed on the parts themselves are the catalogue values and are what a printer and a listing read. cad/measure/filament-value.md measures both ends of it. Every visual judgement in this build, the blind review included, was made on those double-encoded images; that is a limitation of this build's evidence.

The renders are flat-shaded with no ground plane and no shadows. A black disc comes out as a featureless silhouette, the two storage trays read as floating because nothing under them is drawn, and the seven-segment numerals sit on the disc wall facing the two seated players, so at the product's own oblique frame they are turned nearly side-on and cannot be read. All of that is the renderer rather than the solids; the numerals read correctly in the per-world frames under cad/snap/worlds/.

Jupiter, Saturn, Neptune and Uranus were reviewed against their references and deliberately kept as they are. Their bands, their spot and their streaks are finished work rather than an unfinished job: a band system and a storm in an atmosphere really are a belt of latitude and a round patch.
This set is not published by this run and carries no published name. Antisol Hesper is a working title for an unpublished revision.

An independent reviewer of this build's images disagrees with one choice the correction brief made, and the disagreement is recorded rather than buried. In their words: the Magellan reference's bright highland terrain measures hue 38 degrees at saturation 0.66 against a ground of hue 30 at 0.83, so on the real planet the bright terrain is warmer and yellower than the ground it sits on; beige #F7E6DE is hue 19 at saturation 0.10 against a globe of #FFB549 at hue 36, so the piece's bright tone is pinker and cooler than its globe. The hue relationship is inverted relative to the reference. The brief names beige, so this build kept it. cad/measure/venus-highland-palette.md checks all nineteen stocked filaments and finds only one that is brighter than the globe, warm and chromatic -- yellow #FFD834 -- which separates 9.6 greyscale levels from the globe in the canonical render against beige's 20.2, the weakest marking separation in the set, and which is Saturn's own globe filament. The objection is a real limit of the filament range and cannot be fixed with the plastics this shop stocks.

Asked directly whether the piece reads as the same planet as the Magellan reference, that reviewer answered no on the Aphrodite face and arguable on the other. They could match the three-tone scheme, the amber ground hue, an elongated bright feature crossing the equatorial zone and dark blotches at middle latitudes. They could not find, and the piece does not carry: the reference's reticulated mesh of branching bright threads, its saturation, its dark terrain as a major constituent, any radiating streak or linear ridge, and any circular corona or impact basin. That is the expected outcome and the brief says so in advance -- the piece is a simplified map of the reference, not the reference.

At the hero framing Venus's globe is 211 pixels across and the lowland occupies 2.8 per cent of it, a single dark smudge at the collar, while the highland occupies 14.9 per cent, so a buyer looking at the hero image sees one marking on Venus. This follows from the planet's geography rather than from the framing: sweeping the single-piece camera through 360 degrees, Aphrodite peaks at 1.00 on the visibility index with the plains at 0.44, and the plains peak at 2.00 with Aphrodite at 0.21. No camera shows both, because Venus's major plains lie on the hemisphere away from Aphrodite. cad/measure/venus-facing.md is that sweep.

On the Aphrodite face -- three of the eight product images -- the lone cocoa wedge reads as a stray polygon rather than as terrain, because it is the only dark marking present, it is clipped flat where the globe enters its collar, and it has no neighbours to belong to. The same material on the opposite face reads immediately as terrain. The clipping is correct behaviour, not a modelling fault.

Aphrodite Terra spans roughly half the globe's circumference rather than most of it: measuring the near-limb annulus degree by degree in the overhead frame, highland occupies 25 per cent of it in four separate arcs, the longest 53 degrees. That follows from the supplied ring data rather than from the build.

In the hero frame Venus's highland band, Saturn's ring and both piece bases read as the same near-white, so the frame's three most prominent light elements are one tone. The pieces remain easy to tell apart by size and by Saturn's ring.
product.summary: Jungle Chess played with the solar system. Every piece is a planet, and a planet's size on the board is the fifth root of its real measured diameter, so rank is something you can see rather than something you have to learn: Mercury is the smallest world in play and Jupiter the largest, and the traditional rules are followed exactly as written. Matter faces antimatter. One army's worlds lean their poles one way and the other army's lean the other, by each planet's own true axial tilt, and the bases give the same answer again in white against black. Four of the eight worlds wear the pattern a telescope shows, as circles and bands. The other four wear a real map: Earth its own coastlines, Mars its own dark continents, Mercury its smooth plains with the Caloris basin in them, and Venus -- alone in the set -- a surface no eye has ever seen. Venus used to wear its clouds and now wears the ground underneath them, from the Magellan radar map: a golden amber ball with the long sweep of Aphrodite Terra running most of the way round its equator and three dark lowland plains around it, and still upside down, because Venus's axis is tipped 177 degrees and this is the one world in the set whose map reads inverted. A cocoa-brown asteroid belt crosses the middle of the field, a star stands at each end with two flames bursting off the board edge, and the three cells around each star are sunken corona wells where a captured world drops out of the light and its rank counts for nothing. You win by walking one of your worlds onto the rival star.
product.title: Antisol Hesper
product.what_arrives: Forty-two printed parts: sixteen worlds, a board in four panels, twelve asteroid-belt tiles, two stars, six corona cells and two storage trays. Nothing is glued, screwed or assembled; the tiles and stars drop into their own pockets and the panels butt together.
